public_rationale: Texas's October 23, 2026 lawsuit shows continued state litigation over alleged AI harms, but does not establish that states lacked effective preventive alternatives [e3]. The June 2 order establishes a cybersecurity-focused initiative with voluntary review, not the full federal-policy position in October [e1]. The March 20 framework describes broader legislative proposals, not implemented protections [e2]. These records establish neither the relevant federal-policy gap at the time of the Texas lawsuit nor states' practical dependence on reactive litigation [e1, e2, e3]. The forecast therefore remains unresolved.
limitations: The records do not establish whether the relevant federal-policy gap persisted on October 23, 2026.
No evidence establishes the effectiveness or inadequacy of preventive alternatives addressing the same harms.
The Texas announcement reports allegations, not findings that harm occurred.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Until the federal government takes a more comprehensive approach to AI risks, states will have little choice but to file after-the-fact lawsuits against AI companies.
conditions: until the US government takes a more comprehensive approach to AI risks

statement.excerpt: For now, and until the US government takes a more comprehensive approach to addressing AI risks, states will have little choice but to file lawsuits like these; unfortunately, those can only be filed after harms have been caused.
statement.document_title: The White House’s shambolic AI policy

from_speaker: until the US government takes a more comprehensive approach to addressing AI risks
our_interpretation: The claim concerns practical reliance on reactive, harm-based enforcement like Florida's lawsuit. It does not assert that every preventive lawsuit is legally unavailable.

The relevant federal approach must address the consumer and personal harms discussed in the passage. A cybersecurity initiative or a legislative proposal alone does not establish that condition has ended.
An additional lawsuit supports the predicted pattern but does not establish that states had little effective alternative.
The federal-policy condition must be established for the dates of any enforcement events used to resolve the forecast. June evidence cannot establish unchanged policy through October.
criteria.support_condition: While the stated federal-policy gap demonstrably persists, enforcement records show that states practically depend on lawsuits responding to alleged harms because effective preventive alternatives are materially unavailable.
criteria.contradiction_condition: During a verified federal-policy gap, records show that states have effective, practicable preventive alternatives addressing the same harms, materially defeating the claimed dependence on reactive litigation.

evidence.explanation: The order focuses on cybersecurity; Section 3 provides voluntary model review and disclaims mandatory release licensing under that section. This supports the narrow June policy premise, but cannot establish the absence of other protections or unchanged policy through October.

The announcement describes proposals extending beyond cybersecurity, including child protection. It complicates any claim that federal policy addressed nothing else, but does not demonstrate enacted, effective protections.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Attorney General Paxton brings claims'
evidence.publisher: Office of the Attorney General of Texas
evidence.explanation: The official announcement establishes continued state harm-based litigation. Its allegations are not findings that harm occurred, and filing the case does not establish the absence of effective alternatives.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Dated federal-policy and state enforcement records establishing the relevant policy gap at the same time, together with implementation evidence showing either practical dependence on reactive lawsuits or effective preventive alternatives that materially defeat that dependence.
